No witness is mechanically decisive; readings are weighed by date, independence, quality, linguistic fit, contextual fit, and explanatory power.","historical_findings":["The Hebrew and Aramaic consonantal text was transmitted before the full Masoretic system of vowel points and cantillation marks was developed and written into manuscripts.","Written vowel letters such as א, ה, ו, and י are part of the consonantal orthography when present and therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to later vowel points.","The Masoretic points preserve a highly valuable and often ancient reading tradition, but the graphic signs themselves are secondary to the consonantal text.","Masoretic cantillation encodes traditional accentuation, phrasing, syntax, and liturgical reading; it is important interpretive evidence but does not have the same textual status as written consonants.","Unpointed consonantal strings can sometimes permit more than one grammatically possible vocalization, although context and usage often sharply restrict the possibilities.","Biblical manuscripts, parallel texts, Ketiv/Qere notes, and ancient translations attest that more than one textual or reading tradition existed in some passages."],"theological_assumptions":[],"rationale":"The consonants, including written vowel letters, constitute the primary written datum. Masoretic vocalization is later in graphic form but preserves expert traditional interpretation and therefore deserves a strong rebuttable presumption rather than either absolute authority or dismissal. A merely imaginable repointing is insufficient: an alternate must satisfy morphology, syntax, lexicon, historical language, and context, with independent ancient support materially strengthening it. Conversely, because the points are interpretive additions rather than original graphemes, disagreement with the received pointing alone cannot disqualify an otherwise well-supported vocalization.
